comments.text: I knew a kid in middle and high school who had undiagnosed narcolepsy. It was really hard on him, I remember, because he could just never stay awake through classes and teachers were always giving him flack for it assuming it was a behavior issue. Kids would bully him, to the point where some of the bullying was starting to get racist but nothing was done for ages bc everyone just assumed he was a big dumb oaf who was wasting him time all night instead of sleeping and then falling asleep in class. I think his parents were nudged towards looking for the diagnosis by our football coach, who realized there might be something wrong because of how he was doing during practice. But it was really rough seeing how he was treated before he found out the diagnosis to get treatment and accommodation at school.

In childhood one of my friends was a girl who had been adopted from Vietnam. She had received major abdominal surgery due to her intestines not having formed correctly. Unfortunately, she received this surgery late enough in her life that she could still remember it, and all the healing. It definitely marked her. 

I don’t think it gets talked about enough how severely the US affected the Vietnamese population. It is still affecting people there to this day. There’s always focus on the soldiers, but these were just people living their lives under occupation, and having kids who had such severe deformities that the poorer families simply couldn’t care for them. And for the richer ones there was stigma tied to it. These kids were then given up, which IS traumatic for the kids. It’s so sad to me.

I started showing signs of narcolepsy when I was 12, and by 14 the symptoms had become much more obvious. For years, I was misdiagnosed with depression and often told I needed to just push through and work harder. I was finally diagnosed with narcolepsy at 19.

Now, at 30 years old, I still struggle to tell people about my condition and often try to push through my days as if it doesn’t exist. This video is incredibly encouraging, and I want to thank Dr. Mike for helping bring more awareness to narcolepsy.

I hope that one day I can be as confident and open about my condition as the woman in this video. I struggle with mental health and a lot of insecurity that can affect my confidence at work and contribute to financial struggles. It’s hard and psychologically exhausting. 

This video reminds me that it’s possible to live life without being defined by your condition. Narcolepsy will always be a part of my story, but it doesn’t have to control it. Instead of seeing myself as a victim of my condition I want to learn how to work with it, advocate for myself, and help others better understand what living with narcolepsy is really like.

(Btw i LOVE driving and have just learned what can trigger my narcolepsy at those times. I’m an incredibly safe and accident free driver 😉)

Got to thinking about it because of the woman with the seizures - I would love to see a 'what to do' educational series from you. Recently my mom started having seizures. Luckily she was already in hospital when it occurred, but it got me thinking about it and I realized how I'd have no idea how to handle the situation, apart from calling emergency services, if I had been alone with her. 

I can think of dozens of situations like that, where I'd have no idea what to do: Someone having a seizure, heart attack, stroke, choking (especially with a child/infant), amongst so many other things. Of course the obvious answer is to call emergency services, however, the time between the event and getting someone on the line can be crucial in making sure someone ends up alright. On top of that, knowing ahead of time what to look for and what to communicate to the dispatcher could really help to improve communication and understanding in a stressful situation.

If anyone could make a series like this, who could reach the most people and clearly communicate it, I know it would be you.

Great to see some awareness being raised about narcolepsy. I have the condition myself, including cataplexy.
It all started when I was around 12 or 13 years old. My symptoms gradually got worse over time until one day my mom saw something about narcolepsy on TV and recognized the signs. We contacted a professor who specialized in the condition, and we were contacted back almost immediately. A few weeks later, I underwent the sleep tests. I'm 28 now, and I'm incredibly grateful that there are medications available. I take Xyrem and clomipramine, which help me sleep much better at night and significantly reduce my cataplexy attacks during the day.

I can honestly say that without these medications, I wouldn't have been able to enjoy life or even keep a job because my cataplexy was so severe.

comments.text:
I have FND, and the worst part of the condition is how unresearched, and misunderstood it is, especially by doctors. Just because current methods of testing can't be used to determine what is causing the symptoms, doesn't mean there isn't a reason or that it isn't impacting someone’s quality of life. I first had a seizure walking down the stairs of my house, which caused me to black out and fall to the bottom of the staircase. As with other forms of seizures, there can be lengthy post-ictal phase, where I am often confused about what has happened. This typically is accompanied by inability to communicate verbally, and sometimes lack of feeling or ability to move one side of my body. 

When the paramedics came they immediately thought that since I had a history of mental health issues that I must have jumped down the stairs in an effort to hurt myself (I know mental health can be irrational at times, but I feel like jumping down 1 flight of stairs would be a very round about way of self-harm). Due to the assumptions they made, they refused to take my symptoms seriously, insisting that I should simply get up and walk to the ambulance (which required walking back up the stairs), despite this being the first seizure I had ever had, and that I was unable to feel one side of my body. When I got to the emergency room the first nurse that came to see me didn't seem to have been told accurately what happened, and once she realised that I potentially had a seizure, as well as fallen down a flight of stairs, she immediately put  C-collar on me. 

The doctors ran a bunch of tests to rule out MS and such, but once they ruled those things out, they simply sent me home without any follow up care, despite the fact that I was having between 5-20 seizures a day, and was bed-bound. My parents took me back to the hospital after a few days without improvement, and I was then put into a physical rehab ward to try to learn to walk again. After much physio, I was able to regain feeling in my limbs, but the seizures continued. I want to preface that my experience is only reflective of the healthcare system where I am from, which is outside of the US. Though medical gaslighting and dismissal seems to be an issue regardless of country.

Despite seeing multiple neurologists, I have frequently been dismissed and told there is nothing they can do, and that the only thing that could help is therapy. I have tried to explain that I have been in therapy since I was 14, which was years prior to my symptoms, and that ongoing therapy has not had a direct impact on my symptoms. Several years later I spoke to a different neurologist about my symptoms, and they redid an EEG, which failed to capture a seizure, but was sufficient enough for the doctor to say it was non-epileptiform seizures and that there was no treatment for that. 

Due to how I have been treated by doctors repeatedly, I now don't mention that I am diagnosed with FND, as in my experience, doctor almost always lose concern or care when they see that in your chart, even when talking about unrelated symptoms or medical conditions. It is incredibly sad that just mentioning an FND diagnosis will cause most doctors to dismiss you, assume your symptoms are psychosomatic or all in your head, and refuse to offer any management avenues.

I really hope one day that doctors learn to be more comfortable saying, "I don't know", instead of invalidating and dismissing real symptoms people are experiencing. I have several other physical health issues, including a genetic condition that went undiagnosed for 23 years, despite having symptoms and chronic pain since I was born. We need to learn more compassion for each other, and make less assumptions or judgements. You never truly know what someone is struggling with. Many disabilities are invisible. Be kind!
